passage: I'm Pema, and I sit two benches behind Varun. Every time Varun answered a question, the bigger boy from 7C laughed loudly and copied his voice in a squeak. The back row kept glancing over, waiting. Varun's ears went red and his hands stayed still on the desk. I thought he would snap or cry. Instead he finished his sentence, packed his bag, and walked to the front bench near the teacher, without looking at the boy. At lunch I saw him talking to the class teacher. I can't tell what he was really feeling, but the boy stopped getting his laugh.

qa.q: Where did Varun move to after the boy laughed?
qa.a: He walked to the front bench near the teacher.

qa.q: What might Varun have been feeling, judging by his red ears and still hands?
qa.a: He was probably hurt or embarrassed, but Pema cannot be sure; finishing his sentence and walking away suggests he chose not to give the boy a reaction.

qa.q: What could Varun keep doing if the name-calling starts again?
qa.a: He can keep moving away, stay near the teacher and friends, and tell an adult again if it continues, since the boy's words do not say anything true about him.

qa.q: How might the bigger boy see the moment when Varun does not react?
qa.a: He may feel his laugh has lost its point, because the back row stopped waiting and he no longer got the reaction he wanted.

grounding: A classmate observes a bullied boy refusing to give a reaction, moving away and speaking to the teacher.

passage:
I'm Francis, and I remember the term a big boy in Class 7 decided my voice was funny. Whenever I answered in class, he snorted and said "Squeaky" loud enough for the back row. They always turned to watch me, waiting.
At first my face went hot and I stopped putting my hand up. Then I saw it: he only did it when people were watching. He wanted a show.
So I stopped giving one. I finished my answer calmly. I moved to the front bench. And after class, with Hafsa beside me, I told our class teacher. She moved him to another row that week and spoke to him.
His name for me wasn't the truth about me. It was only noise.

qa.q: What did the big boy call Francis?
How did Francis feel when the back row turned to watch?
qa.a: Francis felt embarrassed and small, with a hot face, and stopped putting a hand up for a while.

qa.q: Which choices helped Francis most, and why?
qa.a: Staying calm, moving to the front bench and telling the class teacher with Hafsa, because it denied the boy his show and brought in an adult who moved him.

qa.q: How might the big boy have felt when Francis stopped reacting?
qa.a: The big boy may have felt frustrated or bored, since the laughter and attention he wanted were no longer coming.

grounding: A child is mocked whenever they speak by a bigger boy who wants an audience; they keep their dignity, move away and tell an adult.

passage:
Note from the class teacher, Class 5A.
For two weeks, a bigger boy, Nitin, has been laughing loudly whenever Pallavi speaks and calling her "duck face". He glances round each time to see who is watching.
Pallavi's hands trembled at first, and she stopped raising her hand. This week I saw a change. She kept her voice steady, finished her answer, and did not look at him. At break she moved to a bench near the library.
Yesterday she came to me and said quietly, "I don't want to fight. I just want it to stop." I thanked her for telling me and spoke to Nitin and his parents that afternoon. Her seat is now next to the window.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi move to at break?
What does Pallavi's steady voice this week suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests that although she still felt hurt, she had decided not to give Nitin the reaction he wanted, which took quiet courage.

qa.q: What did the teacher do after Pallavi spoke up?
qa.a: The teacher thanked her, spoke to Nitin and his parents that same afternoon, and moved her seat.

qa.q: What is Nitin looking for when he glances round?
qa.a: Nitin is looking for an audience, since he checks who is watching every time he laughs.

grounding: A bigger boy calls a girl names and laughs when she speaks to get an audience; she keeps her dignity, moves away and tells an adult.
